timeline.body:
Fixes #3054

RELNOTES: Options specified on the pseudo-command `common` in `.rc` files are now ignored by commands that do not support them as long as they are valid options for *any* Bazel command. Previously, commands that did not support all options given for `common` would fail to run. These previous semantics of `common` are now available via the new `always` pseudo-command.
@haxorz If time permits, could you perhaps give early feedback on the general approach taken by this PR? It doesn't come with tests or user-facing docs yet, but should otherwise be fully functional.
If we used a `Set<Class>` rather than `List<Class>` could we then get rid of the `allowDuplicatesParsingEquivalently` and `#equivalentForParsing` stuff?

reply.body:
Good point, we should add a `.distinct()` here to make the cache key smaller.

I don't think that passing to a `Set` would reduce the overall complexity of this PR though: The problem isn't that option *classes* collide, it's that individual options can collide across classes. For example, both `cquery` and `query` define an `--output` flag, but those flag definition are distinct and differ in certain aspects (e.g. the allowed values). However, crucially, both options accept an argument (that is, are neither boolean nor Void options) and hence parse identically, as checked by `equivalentForParsing`. That's why this PR introduces an additional type of equality that is more lenient than `Object#equals` for `OptionDefinition`s.
Thanks that wasn't clear to me. Hmm that is an annoying bit of necessary complexity of this FR.

I would definitely add more comments as part of polishing this PR if you approve of the approach.

I agree that this additional complexity is annoying, but if it isn't taken care of by Bazel itself, it is pushed onto end users. I actually think that compared to the level of effort required to manually apply flags to all commands they are valid for, the complexity of `OptionsParserImpl#equivalentForParsing` is comparatively contained.

> For example, both cquery and query define an --output flag ... However, crucially, both options

What would happen if they weren't equivalent for parsing?

> However, crucially, both options accept an argument (that is, are neither boolean nor Void options) and hence parse identically

What would be wrong with two different options with the same name that were both booleans?

> What would happen if they weren't equivalent for parsing?

That would result in an error when `all-supported` is used. This error could be caught by tests. It does restrict what options Bazel commands can provide to some extent, but I see that as necessary to support this feature.

> What would be wrong with two different options with the same name that were both booleans?

That would also work. It would only error if one is a boolean and the other accepts a value.

Okay I approve of the approach.

> That would result in an error when all-supported is used. This error could be caught by tests. It does restrict what options Bazel commands can provide to some extent, but I see that as necessary to support this feature.

Thanks that's what I figured. Agree this restriction to the codebase is a sensible requirement for this FR. Please make this clear in a code comment.

> That would also work. It would only error if one is a boolean and the other accepts a value.

Sounds good. I see that `#equivalentForParsing` handles this. I was moreso questioning the phrasing of your PR comment.

I'm not clear on why we're doing the `equivalentForParsing` check, especially because it seems like a very loose check. For example, if `some_option` accepts different values in different commands (such as two different enums), the check passes correct? What are we trying to guard against exactly?

timeline.message:
Support `all-supported` pseudo command in rc files

Options specified on the `all-supported` command in rc files are applied
to all commands that support them. If an option isn't supported by the
current command but by some other Bazel command, it is ignored. If it
isn't supported by any Bazel command, the usual error message is shown.
timeline.author: Fabian Meumertzheim

 -   `startup`: startup options, which go before the command, and are described

--   `common`: options that apply to all Bazel commands.
+-   `common`: options that apply to all Bazel commands. If a command does not

+-   `all-supported`: options that should be applied to all Bazel commands that

 -   _`command`_: Bazel command, such as `build` or `query` to which the options

+  def testCanOverrideStarlarkFlagInBazelrcConfigStanza(self):
+    self.ScratchFile("WORKSPACE.bazel")
+    self.ScratchFile("bazelrc", [
+        "build:red --//f:color=red",
+    ])
+    self.ScratchFile("f/BUILD.bazel", [
+        'load(":f.bzl", "color", "r")',
+        "color(",
+        '    name = "color",',
+        '    build_setting_default = "white",',
+        ")",
+        'r(name = "r")',
+    ])
+    self.ScratchFile("f/f.bzl", [
+        'ColorValue = provider("color")',
+        "def _color_impl(ctx):",
+        "    return [ColorValue(color = ctx.build_setting_value)]",
+        "color = rule(",
+        "    implementation = _color_impl,",
+        "build_setting = config.string(flag = True),",
+        ")",
+        "def _r_impl(ctx):",
+        "    print(ctx.attr._color[ColorValue].color)",
+        "    return [DefaultInfo()]",
+        "r = rule(",
+        "    implementation = _r_impl,",
+        '    attrs = {"_color": attr.label(default = "//f:color")},',
+        ")",
+    ])
+
+    _, _, stderr = self.RunBazel([
+        "--bazelrc=bazelrc",
+        "build",
+        "--nobuild",
+        "//f:r",
+        "--config=red",
+        "--//f:color=green",
+    ])
+    self.assertTrue(

+    _, _, stderr = self.RunBazel([

+        "build",
+        "--nobuild",
+        "//f:r",
+        "--//f:color=green",
+        "--config=red",
+    ])
+    self.assertTrue(
+        any("/f/f.bzl:9:10: red" in line for line in stderr),
+        "\n".join(stderr),
+    )
+
+  def testAllSupportedPseudoCommand(self):
+    self.ScratchFile("WORKSPACE.bazel")
+    self.ScratchFile(".bazelrc", [
+      "all-supported --copt=-Dfoo",
+      "all-supported --copt -Dbar",
+      "all-supported:my-config --copt=-Dbaz",
+      "all-supported:my-config --copt -Dquz",
+    ])
+    self.ScratchFile("pkg/BUILD.bazel", [
+      "cc_binary(name='main',srcs=['main.cc'])",
+    ])
+    self.ScratchFile("pkg/main.cc", [
+      "#include <stdio.h>",
+      "int main() {",
+      "#ifdef foo",
+      "  printf(\"foo\\n\");",
+      "#endif",
+      "#ifdef bar",
+      "  printf(\"bar\\n\");",
+      "#endif",
+      "#ifdef baz",
+      "  printf(\"baz\\n\");",
+      "#endif",
+      "#ifdef quz",
+      "  printf(\"quz\\n\");",
+      "#endif",
+      "  return 0;",
+      "}",
+    ])
+
+    # Check that run honors the all-supported flags.
+    _, stdout, _ = self.RunBazel([
+      "run",
+      "//pkg:main",
+    ])
+    self.assertEquals(
+        ["foo", "bar"],
+        stdout,
+    )
+
+    _, stdout, _ = self.RunBazel([
+      "run",
+      "--config=my-config",
+      "//pkg:main",
+    ])
+    self.assertEquals(
+        ["foo", "bar", "baz", "quz"],
+        stdout,
+    )
+
+    # Check that query ignores the unsupported all-supported flags.
+    _, stdout, _ = self.RunBazel([
+      "query",
+      "//pkg:main",
+    ])
+
+    _, stdout, _ = self.RunBazel([
+      "query",
+      "--config=my-config",
+      "//pkg:main",
+    ])
+
+  def testAllSupportedPseudoCommand_unsupportedOptionValue(self):
+    self.ScratchFile("WORKSPACE.bazel")
+    self.ScratchFile(".bazelrc", [
+      "all-supported --output=starlark",
+    ])
+    self.ScratchFile("pkg/BUILD.bazel", [
+      "cc_binary(name='main',srcs=['main.cc'])",
+    ])
+
+    # Check that cquery honors the all-supported flag.
+    _, stdout, _ = self.RunBazel([
+      "cquery",
+      "--starlark:expr=target.label.name",
+      "//pkg:main",
+    ])
+    self.assertEquals(
+        ["main"],
+        stdout,
+    )
+
+    # Check that query fails as it supports the --output flag, but not its
+    # value.
+    exit_code, stdout, stderr = self.RunBazel([
+      "query",
+      "//pkg:main",
+    ], allow_failure = True)
+    self.AssertExitCode(exit_code, 2, stderr)
+    self.assertTrue(
+        any("ERROR: Invalid output format 'starlark'." in line for line in stderr),
+        stderr,
+    )
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+  unittest.main()

timeline.body: @justinhorvitz I pushed a new commit that adds comments, including detailed examples of `OptionDefinition`s that do and do not parse equivalently. I hope that this clears up the purpose of the function.

> @justinhorvitz I pushed a new commit that adds comments, including detailed examples of `OptionDefinition`s that do and do not parse equivalently. I hope that this clears up the purpose of the function.

Your latest comments make the ambiguous parsing issue more clear, thanks. What I'm still missing is why that's something we now need to check when an `all-supported` line is used in an rc file. Why is ambiguous parsing only an issue in that case, and not say for a `common` rc line?

> Your latest comments make the ambiguous parsing issue more clear, thanks. What I'm still missing is why that's something we now need to check when an `all-supported` line is used in an rc file. Why is ambiguous parsing only an issue in that case, and not say for a `common` rc line?

The difference is that with `common`, we still only load `OptionsData` for `common` + the current command, where we know that there won't be different `OptionsDefinition`s with the same name. This has always been enforced in `IsolatedOptionsData#from`.

With `all-supported`, we now need to load the `OptionsData` for *all* commands and thus necessarily get into a situation where there now are `OptionsDefinition`s that are non-equal but share a name. That is where the `equivalentForParsing` equivalence relation comes into play: It's weaker than equality, but strong enough that parsing `OptionsDefinition`s that conflict in name is still possible unambiguously.

Please let me know if I can clarify this further.

> With `all-supported`, we now need to load the `OptionsData` for _all_ commands 

Do we only "need" to load all of the data because we wish to make it an error when an option name isn't recognized for any command? If we tolerated `all-supported --option_that_never_exists` would we still need to load the `OptionsData` for all commands? (I'm not implying that we should tolerate that, I'm just trying to understand the full tradeoff before forming an opinion).

> That is where the `equivalentForParsing` equivalence relation comes into play: It's weaker than equality, but strong enough that parsing `OptionsDefinition`s that conflict in name is still possible unambiguously.

Why does it matter that two options are `equivalentForParsing` if only one of the options is relevant for the current command?

> Do we only "need" to load all of the data because we wish to make it an error when an option name isn't recognized for any command? If we tolerated `all-supported --option_that_never_exists` would we still need to load the `OptionsData` for all commands? (I'm not implying that we should tolerate that, I'm just trying to understand the full tradeoff before forming an opinion).

I don't think we could just tolerate `all-supported --option_not_on_the_current_command` even if we deemed that tolerable since we do not know how to continue parsing the rest of the rc file after an option for which we don't have the `OptionsData`: If `--option_not_on_the_current_command` is defined on some command and expects a value, we need to skip the following argument before we continue parsing. If it is e.g. a boolean option on some other command, then we must not skip the following argument as a boolean option doesn't consume an additional argument. Without `OptionsData`, in particular for completely unknown options, we decide between the two cases.

> Why does it matter that two options are `equivalentForParsing` if only one of the options is relevant for the current command?

Similar answer to above: It doesn't actually matter for the current command, but it would mean that the rest of the rc file would parse differently depending on which command it is applied to, which seems extremely error prone.

timeline.body: I added the test.

Is bike-shedding still welcome on the command name? Was there a definitive discussion somewhere?

The name `all-supported` sounds retrofitted to me - if it had been included in the original design I feel it would have been shorter. After all I expect most users will just start using this new pseudo-command as their default behavior because it's so much easier to use.

@pjjw said:
> all-effective?
> apply?
> any? (lil proto joke)

4. `all`, because it's already a Bazel wild-card in the target syntax (`//path/to/package:all`)
5. `*` for the same reason, and also it's less likely to be picked up by existing RC file parsers (which could be both good and bad)

It's never too late for bikeshedding ;⁠-⁠) I would personally welcome as much input as we can get.

I would prefer a name that makes it clear what the difference to `common` is - I do see value in using `common` even with this new pseudo-command being available. That's why I'm not fully convinced that something as short as `all` or `any` is precise enough, but I agree that `all-supported` is quite verbose.

> 4. `all`, because it's already a Bazel wild-card in the target syntax (`//path/to/package:all`)

+1 to a one word name, `all` is good or maybe `supported`.

A few more:
- _applicable_
- _appropriate_
- _congruent_
- _matching_
- _understood_

I learned something from `cquery` vs `query`. In almost all cases, `cquery` is the better thing for users to use, because it's generally faster to follow only one branch of configurable rule definitions and users didn't really intend to run an "unconfigured" query. However it's reasonable to assume that the shorter name is the "thing you're supposed to use" and the longer name is for special cases where "you need to do something different". I have to make this point every time I do a Bazel training.

My concern with any of the long names is that users will still have to go through the painful discovery that `common` doesn't do the intuitive thing "just use these flags", as well as the footgun with `build` flags not applying to `query` that is discussed on #3054 

So if we agree that most new users should default their behavior to this new affordance, I think we should make it really short, not just one word.
What about the ever-adaptive underscore (`_`)? Can that serve as the command placeholder?
I vote for either * or all. I think I would prefer * since it is commonly used in these kind of scenarios.
i like all, definitely.

timeline.body:
The result of the discussion in https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/3054 was that we no longer need to search for a new name as we can just change the behavior of the existing `common` pseudo-command, with the big advantage that no one has to learn a new name or change all `common` lines in rc files.

@justinhorvitz @haxorz I pushed three new commits to realize https://github.com/bazelbuild/bazel/issues/3054#issuecomment-1540945289 and updated the PR description with RELNOTES, please take a look. Since this will now be used by default with existing rc files, I wanted to make sure its effects are more visible and thus added logging with `--announce_rc`.
I like this direction a lot, thanks for updating!
@justinhorvitz @haxorz Friendly ping
If the option name is unrecognized for any bazel command, will it fail?
